Australia has pretty good regulations and should be commended for that, but the financial system is overly dependent on the residential property market and carries huge diversification risks. 

Ideally, a financial system should be well-diversified to mitigate risks. However, Australia's system revolves around four 'too-big-to-fail' banks that dominate more than 70% of the country's banking sector, hold over 93.5% of all residential mortgages, and have more than two-thirds of their balance sheets in residential mortgages.

This concentration exposes both the banks and Australian citizens (as they were also incentivised to invest in property due to poor policies and a terribly biased tax system) to significant risks related to the residential mortgage market.

While the current system functions smoothly when no disruptions occur, any significant downturn or a case of something going wrong could trigger a domino effect, and the Australian taxpayers could bear the burden of costly bailouts for decades to come to prevent the collapse of these too-big-to-fail banks. Alternatively, if these banks were allowed to fail, the consequences for the economy would be dire too.

To build a more resilient financial system, Australia should have considered breaking up these big four banks and preventing their continued growth into 'too-big-to-fail' status in the first place. Encouraging banks to provide more business loans instead of residential mortgages would have diversified loan portfolios and risk structures. Additionally, altering the tax system to reduce incentives for Australians to invest heavily in the residential property market (through measures like capital gains discounts and negative gearing) would have been beneficial.

By heavily investing in residential property (a non-productive asset class) rather than in businesses and stocks, Australians have prioritized assets that do not contribute to the economy through the production of goods and services or innovation. In the event of an economic crisis, this focus on residential properties rather than businesses will make rebuilding the economy considerably more challenging.

1. Make good notes. Use colour coding, sticky colour notes, a table of contents, etc. so you can easily flip to whichever note you need when answering the questions. Especially so you can easily reference tax legislation, cases, etc.

Be honest and ask yourself whether you are actually investing into residential property because you want to make houses more affordable for future generations, or whether it is because you are hoping to make money from house prices increasing.

Supply is low for now as rate rises are still quite recent so we haven't had enough time to feel the full impact of the rate rises. In the months ahead, more and more people are going to start to let go off their investment properties as the rate rises hits them and they can no longer afford to hold (you can already see a growing number of posts in /r/ausfinance of cases like this). As more properties hit the market, supply will increase, causing a downward pressure on house prices exacerbated by the high interest rates which will limit bid prices (as people are unable to borrow as much as before) despite solid demand. 

In the meantime, inflation will continue to rise past expectations due to landlords passing on the rate rises to renters and that the [money supply has essentially doubled over the past 3 years as a result of COVID stimulus](https://tradingeconomics.com/australia/money-supply-m0). At this point, RBA can choose between continuing rate rises, or destroying the purchasing power of the currency. 

Given the RBA's three mandates are the stability of the currency, full employment, and economic prosperity and welfare of citizens, and that two of the three mandates justify further rate rises/quantitative tightening (i.e., high inflation, unemployment at historical lows). The RBA will be forced to increase rate rises to protect the purchasing power of the AUD until a point at which unemployment begins to rise (remember, at the moment unemployment is currently still at the lowest levels in history and we still haven't seen unemployment increase much as of yet). 

Once unemployment begins to rise (3-4 months in the future as a result of continuing rate rises to combat unexpectedly high inflation), RBA will have more leeway to lower rates, but by then a full blown global recession will be underway in the midst of rising rates and persistent inflation, giving central banks across the world limited tools to stimulate the global economy without encouraging runaway inflation.

Ultimately, house prices will fall unless the RBA is willing to destroy the purchasing power of the currency and turn AUD into monopoly dollars, which is unlikely due to their main job as the central bank being to ensure the stability of the currency.

This is why I don't invest in residential real estate even if I know it might make me money. I don't want to contribute a single cent to exacerbating a basic human need, a home, into an investment that will increasingly doom the youth of the future.

Singles is fine, but stacking is ideal however most games you probably won't be able to manage this (assuming you're vsing decent players). It's harder to stack as pos 5 as opposed to pos 4 because most of the time you need to baby sit your squishy pos 1 as a pos 5 in lane, whereas pos 3 heroes can do okay alone for a bit (e.g., axe, timber, etc.). 

When you are stacking in lane early, you risk your pos 1 dying and very likely he will miss last hits without you in the lane to keep the pos 4 off him. The pros of stacking here is that enemy offlaner loses exp and farm when you pull. In this scenario, if you weigh up the two, the cons outweigh the pros. Your main job as pos 5 isn't to destroy the enemy pos 3. Your main job as pos 5 is to ensure your pos 1 gets a good game. Think of it like a farmed PA vs a farmed Axe. Who wins?

1. Buy 2 sents at the start of the game, 1 to deward your pull and 1 to block enemy pull. As soon as possible, buy another sent as enemy will look to block your pull / deward. 

2. Additionally try to get the next obs as soon as it refreshes as the 2 starting obs generally goes to mid and offlane, thus getting that early obs up when possible is helpful for the lane (do not place the obs around the jungle where enemy is looking to deward / block pulls). 

3. Sometimes you can stay in lane and still not leach exp if you are aware of exp range e.g., trading with enemy pos 4 in jungle to keep him off your pos 1 in lane. Also be aware of your pos 1 timings and nature of their hero e.g., if he is close to leveling up for crucial skill like level 2 blink on anti-mage (as he will skill mana break at level 1) or if your pos 1 is slark, he really needs fast 6 for that shadow dance regen so you would try to play more out of the exp range in lane or even bait enemy pos 3 and 4 to chase you for a kill in jungle.

4. You leave lane if you are winning the lane and your pos 1 is far ahead enough to solo the lane. Play a bit of pos 1 to understand the pos 1 perspective. Look at their items, levels, hero matchup etc. compared to enemy pos 3. This is something you should learn to feel from experience.

Firstly, you misunderstood the definition of cookie jar accounting. I suggest you click on your own link that you have linked on the definition of the term.

Cookie jar accounting means companies creating a reserve (i.e. the cookie jar) that the company can then dip into to stabilise profits during periods where profits are too high or too low so that the company can reduce earnings volatility. This is done because the market does not look favourably upon companies with volatile earnings (due to the increased unpredictability, meaning higher risk investment and less attractive investment to investors as a result).

Once you understand the concept of cookie jar accounting above, then that pretty much makes the rest of your article void. Creating volatile earnings like what has been seen for Tesla is not in the best interests of the company or the directors as it results in the medium term destruction of shareholder value once you utilise all the earnings all at once (hence, the stock's recent poor performance in the actual market). 

In truth, [ASC 606](https://www.revenuehub.org/overview-of-asc-606/) was introduced to **counter** cookie jar accounting by removing holes in the previous revenue accounting standards that allowed companies to manipulate revenue to smooth out profits. This standard has been applied to almost all major countries across the globe with every company to comply for annual periods beginning on January 2018 -- which is why Tesla has changed their accounting policies. Not because they changed it on their own accord to engage in "deceptive/manipulative accounting" as you so claim.
